# Code guide

This guide explains the whole project in the order the code runs: what each file is for, what goes in and comes
out, how the important functions work, and why they were written that way. For the exact signature and docstring
of every function, see `API_REFERENCE.md`, which is generated from the source.

**Keeping this document current.** `API_REFERENCE.md` is regenerated by `python scripts/build_api_reference.py`,
and a test fails if it is out of date. This guide is written by hand: when a stage, a file or a design decision
changes, the matching section here changes in the same commit.

## 1. The idea in one page

PM2.5 is fine particulate matter, measured in micrograms per cubic metre (µg/m³). The US Environmental Protection
Agency publishes hourly readings from regulatory monitors. Above 35.4 µg/m³ averaged over a day, air is classed as
"unhealthy for sensitive groups".

In June 2023, smoke from Canadian wildfires covered the eastern United States. The models in this project are
trained on data that ends in mid-2022, so they have never seen anything like it. They are then asked to forecast
every day of 2023 and 2024. Comparing them answers the question: what kind of forecast keeps working when the data
change?

Every model does the same job. Once a day, at 12:00 UTC, at each of 538 monitors, it looks at no more than the last
168 hours (one week) and predicts the next 48 hours. Most models predict nine quantiles (the 10th to 90th
percentile) for each hour, which gives both a best guess (the median) and a range.

## 2. How the pieces fit together

```
python run.py <stage> [<stage> ...]        run.py looks each name up in pipeline.STAGES

download   EPA zip files            ->  .cache/raw/
panel      raw files                ->  data/processed/panel.npz, stations.csv
eda        panel                    ->  outputs/tables/eda*.{json,csv}, figures 01-05
naive      panel                    ->  forecast store: Persistence, Seasonal naive, Damped persistence
tune       panel                    ->  outputs/tables/gbm_tuning.json
gbm        panel (+ tuning result)  ->  forecast store: three XGBoost variants; gbm_training.json
neural     panel                    ->  forecast store: two transformer variants; neural_training.json
foundation panel                    ->  forecast store: Chronos-Bolt and TimesFM variants (optional)
ensemble   forecast store           ->  forecast store: Ensemble
evaluate   forecast store + panel   ->  scores_*.csv, mae_by_horizon_*.csv, bias_by_outcome.csv, bootstrap
uncertainty forecast store + panel  ->  intervals.csv, intervals_monthly.csv
alerts     forecast store + panel   ->  alerts.csv, alerts_detail.json
figures    tables + forecast store  ->  figures 06-13
report     tables + figures         ->  outputs/report.html
dashboard  tables + forecast store  ->  dashboard/data.js, states.js, index.html
```

Two rules keep this simple:

- **Models never talk to each other.** Each model writes its forecast to the store in one fixed shape. Scoring,
  intervals, alerts, figures and the report read only the store and the tables. Adding a model therefore needs no
  change to any scoring code.
- **Every number in the report is read from a table.** `report.py` contains no results, only sentences with
  placeholders, so the write-up cannot disagree with what was computed.

`src/smokeshift/config.py` holds every path and every design constant (years, split dates, context length, horizon,
quantile levels, the 35.4 threshold). Changing the experiment means changing that file.

"The forecast store" and "the cache" in this guide mean the `.cache` folder inside the project: `.cache/raw` for
downloads, `.cache/forecasts` for every model's output, `.cache/models` for trained models and
`.cache/huggingface` for pretrained weights. Git ignores it, and everything in it can be regenerated.
`docs/INSTALLED.md` lists sizes and how to remove each part.

## 3. The three data structures everything uses

**The panel** is a matrix `values[monitor, hour]` of shape 538 by 35,064, in µg/m³, with `NaN` where a monitor did
not report. Hours are in GMT so that a column means the same instant at every monitor. `bench.Bench` wraps it
together with the list of timestamps (`hours`) and the monitor table (`stations`).

**The forecast grid** is an array `[monitor, issue day, horizon]`: 538 monitors, 729 issue days in the test period,
48 horizons. A quantile forecast has a fourth axis of nine levels. Every model's output has exactly this shape, so
two models can be compared cell by cell. `bench.Bench.targets` returns the truth on the same grid.

**Masks** are boolean arrays on the grid that say which cells count. `bench.Bench.eligible` marks forecasts that
are required (the monitor was mostly reporting). `metrics.regimes` builds the slices used throughout:

| Mask | Meaning | Defined by |
|---|---|---|
| All hours | truth observed and forecast required | data availability |
| Calm at issue | no reading above 35.4 in the 24 hours before the forecast | information at forecast time |
| Smoke at issue | at least one such reading | information at forecast time |
| Elevated hours | the hour being forecast turned out above 35.4 | the outcome |
| Onsets | elevated hour, and it was calm at issue | the outcome |

The distinction in the last column is the most important idea in the evaluation. Slices defined at forecast time
are fair, because a forecaster could be told which one applies. Slices defined by the outcome reward any forecast
that leans high, so they are shown as diagnostics and never used to rank models.

## 4. Stage by stage

### 4.1 `download.py`: get the raw data

`fetch(year)` downloads one EPA file (`hourly_88101_<year>.zip`, 63 to 73 MB) into the cache folder, writing to a
`.part` file first and renaming only when the size matches, so an interrupted download is never mistaken for a
complete one. `fetch_states` gets the 115 kB file of state outlines used by the dashboard map. `run` fetches all
years and writes each file's size and SHA-256 checksum to `data/processed/raw_manifest.json`, which is how someone
else can confirm they have the same input.

### 4.2 `panel.py`: from 35.6 million rows to one matrix

The raw files have one row per instrument per hour, with both local and GMT timestamps.

`_read_year` reads a zip in chunks of two million rows so memory stays bounded. For each chunk it keeps the
contiguous United States, builds a site key from the state, county and site codes, converts the GMT date and time
to an hour index (hours since 1 January 2021), drops readings outside -10 to 1000 µg/m³, and finally averages
instruments that share a site. Dates are converted through their category codes, which is much faster than parsing
millions of date strings.

`build` places all years into one matrix, computes each monitor's share of reported hours per year, and keeps
monitors with at least 85% in every year: 538 of 954. It also assembles the monitor table with location, Census
region, and per-year summaries.

`save` stores the matrix as tenths of a µg/m³ in 16-bit integers with -32768 for missing, which makes the file
17 MB instead of 75 MB. `load` reverses that.

Decisions worth knowing:

- Small negative readings are kept. They are instrument noise around zero, and deleting them would bias clean-air
  averages upwards.
- Nothing is filled in. A missing hour stays missing all the way to scoring.

### 4.3 `bench.py`: the rules of the benchmark

`Bench.issue_times(split)` returns the hour indices at which forecasts are made in the train, validation or test
period. A time belongs to a period only if its whole 48-hour target window does, which guarantees that no training
target overlaps a validation or test target.

`Bench.context(t_idx, length)` returns the readings ending at each issue time; `Bench.targets(t_idx)` returns the
48 hours after it. Both use NumPy index arithmetic instead of loops: an array of issue times plus an array of
offsets selects all windows at once.

`Bench.eligible` requires 80% of the context to be present and at least one reading in the last three hours.
`Bench.last_obs` returns the most recent reading within three hours, which several models use as their anchor.

`fill_context` forward-fills gaps along time, and back-fills only a gap at the very start of a window. It is used
for model inputs only.

### 4.4 `eda.py`: what the data say before any model

Each function answers one question:

| Function | Question | Method |
|---|---|---|
| `shift_by_region` | How different was 2023, and where? | summaries by region and year |
| `paired_shift_test` | Is the change real monitor by monitor? | paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test, Holm correction |
| `distribution_distance` | How far did the whole distribution move? | Kolmogorov-Smirnov and Wasserstein distance, tail ratio |
| `weekday_effect_fdr` | Is there a weekday effect at each monitor? | 538 Mann-Whitney tests with Benjamini-Hochberg control |
| `correlogram` | How far apart do monitors stay correlated? | pairwise correlation binned by distance |
| `eof` | What are the dominant spatial patterns? | principal components of the monitor-by-day matrix |
| `plume_lags` | Does smoke reach upwind monitors first? | lagged cross-correlation between cities |

`_anomalies` prepares data for the last three: daily means are log-transformed and standardised per monitor, so
that a dirty site and a clean site contribute equally. `holm` and `benjamini_hochberg` are written out in a few
lines each, because the algorithms are short and seeing them is more useful than calling a library.

### 4.5 `naive.py`: forecasts that need no learning

- `persistence`: the latest reading repeated for 48 hours.
- `seasonal_naive`: the same clock hour on the most recent observed day.
- `DampedPersistence`: `forecast(h) = profile(hour of h) + rho_h * (now - profile(now))`. The profile is the mean
  of each clock hour over the past week (`_profile_and_anomaly`). `rho_h` is one number per horizon, fitted by
  least squares on the training period; it falls from near 1 at one hour to about 0.16 at 48 hours. This is the
  strongest naive method and the reference that all relative scores use.

### 4.6 `spatial.py`: what the neighbours are reading

`distances_and_bearings` computes great-circle distance and compass bearing between every pair of monitors with
the haversine formula. `Neighbours.band` selects neighbours in a distance range and optionally a compass
quadrant; `Neighbours.idw` gives inverse-distance weights.

`masked_mean` and `masked_max` take a weight matrix and the current readings and return, for every monitor, the
weighted mean or the maximum over the neighbours that have a reading. Both are matrix operations over all
monitors and all issue times at once.

`features` returns sixteen numbers per monitor and issue time: mean within 150 and 300 km, maximum within 300 km,
mean and maximum in the 300 to 800 km ring, the share of monitors within 500 km above the threshold, six-hour
trends, means in four compass quadrants, and four of these expressed relative to the monitor's own reading.
`hourly_channels` returns two neighbour series at every hour, for the transformer.

### 4.7 `features.py`: the table the trees learn from

One row is (monitor, issue time, horizon). `base` computes the features that do not depend on the horizon: the
latest reading, lags from 1 to 167 hours, rolling means, maximum, minimum and standard deviation, the share of the
context that is missing, time of day and day of year as sine and cosine, and location. Most are expressed as a
difference from the latest reading, because a tree cannot subtract two columns itself.

`rows` adds the horizon-specific columns: the horizon, the value at the target's clock hour on the latest observed
day, the weekly profile at that hour, the target's local solar time, and whether it falls on a weekend.
`sample_training_rows` picks a few random horizons per issue time (using all 48 would give 100 million rows);
`all_rows` enumerates every horizon for prediction.

The label is the change from the latest reading. The reasoning and the ablation that tests it are described in
the report.

### 4.8 `gbm.py`: gradient-boosted trees

One XGBoost model serves all monitors and all horizons and outputs nine quantiles at once
(`objective="reg:quantileerror"`). `VARIANTS` defines three models that differ in exactly one thing each, so that
two comparisons are controlled: with or without neighbour features, and change or level as the label.

- `device` checks whether XGBoost can use the GPU and falls back to CPU.
- `tune` runs a random search over ten settings on a 700,000-row subsample, scoring on the validation period.
- `fit` trains on about 2.2 million rows with early stopping on the validation period and saves the model.
- `predict` builds features for blocks of 40 issue days at a time to bound memory, predicts all 48 horizons, adds
  the latest reading back for change-label models, and sorts the quantiles so they cannot cross.
- `shap_summary` uses XGBoost's built-in exact TreeSHAP on a sample of test rows and averages absolute
  attributions separately for clean and elevated target hours.

### 4.9 `neural.py`: a transformer written from scratch

`PatchTransformer` cuts the 168-hour input into 21 patches of 8 hours, embeds each patch with a linear layer, adds
one extra token built from calendar and location, passes the 22 tokens through transformer encoder layers, and
maps the flattened result to 48 horizons by 9 quantiles.

Three choices matter more than the layer count:

1. **asinh scale.** `to_z` maps concentrations with `asinh(x / 5)`, which is close to linear near zero and
   logarithmic for large values. Quantiles are unchanged by a monotone transform, so predicting them on this scale
   and mapping back with `from_z` is exact.
2. **Anchoring.** The network outputs a change that is added to the latest reading, so it can follow an episode
   above anything in training.
3. **Masks.** Missing input hours are forward-filled and flagged in a separate channel. Missing targets are
   excluded from the loss in `pinball_loss`.

`Windows` precomputes the transformed, filled input channels for the whole panel once. `Windows.batch` then cuts
any set of windows with index arithmetic, which is fast enough that no data-loader processes are needed.
`Windows.pairs` lists every eligible (monitor, hour) in a split: about 6.6 million for training.

`fit` samples random windows, trains with AdamW and a one-cycle learning-rate schedule, clips gradients, checks the
validation loss after each epoch and keeps the best weights. `PRESETS` holds a small configuration for CPU (1.1
million parameters) and a larger one for GPU (1.6 million); the device is detected automatically. Both were run,
and they reached the same validation loss.

### 4.10 `foundation.py`: pretrained models, used as they come

`MODELS` lists six configurations: Chronos-Bolt and Chronos-2 from Amazon and TimesFM 2.5 from Google, each with
the shared 168-hour context and with a 512-hour "long context" that checks whether the one-week budget holds the
model back. `DEFAULT` names the ones a plain `python run.py foundation` runs; the environment variable
`SMOKESHIFT_FM` selects others.

`_batches` yields the eligible windows in batches. `_chronos` loads a Chronos checkpoint from the Hugging Face Hub
and asks for the nine quantiles; Chronos-Bolt takes a tensor and Chronos-2 a list of series, and both accept
missing values. `_timesfm` does the same for TimesFM, which interpolates gaps itself. `forecast` dispatches on the
model family and returns the quantiles with timing information. Nothing is trained or tuned. If a package is not
installed, `run` reports that and moves on.

One caution belongs with this stage: the models were released in 2024 and 2025 and may have been pretrained on
series from the test years, so their results are not a guaranteed out-of-time test.

### 4.11 `store.py` and the ensembles

`store.save` writes `point.npy`, `quantiles.npy` and `info.json` into one folder per model. `store.load`
memory-maps the arrays, so reading one horizon of one monitor does not load 680 MB.

`pipeline.ensemble_stage` builds two equal-weight averages of quantiles: "Ensemble" (the two neighbour-aware
trained models) and "Ensemble + foundation" (those two plus Chronos-2 and TimesFM). The membership was written
down before any foundation model had been scored, so it is not chosen on the test set. Nothing is fitted.

### 4.12 `metrics.py` and `evaluate.py`: scoring

`evaluate.common_grid` returns the truth and the cells on which every stored model produced a number.
`metrics.ModelScores` computes, for one model in one pass, the error, the absolute error and the pinball loss on
the whole grid; its methods then summarise any mask: `row` gives MAE, bias, MASE and weighted quantile loss,
`by_horizon` gives MAE at each horizon, and `daily_sum` gives per-day totals.

`metrics.bootstrap_relative` takes those per-day totals and resamples whole days 1,000 times to put an interval on
each model's error relative to damped persistence. Resampling days, not individual forecasts, matters: a plume
makes errors at hundreds of monitors on the same day move together, and treating them as independent would make
the intervals far too narrow.

`evaluate.run` loops over models one at a time (never holding two forecasts in memory) and writes all score
tables.

### 4.13 `conformal.py` and `uncertainty.py`: honest intervals

`raw_interval` takes a model's 0.1 and 0.9 quantiles as its 80% interval. `calibrate` measures by how much the
truth fell outside it (`score = max(lower - y, y - upper)`) and widens the interval by a quantile of past scores,
in two ways:

- **static:** scores from the first 60 days only, never refreshed.
- **adaptive:** each monitor's own scores from a sliding 60-day window, with the target level nudged up after
  covered days and down after misses. A forecast for 48 hours ahead is only fully verified two days later, so the
  update uses scores from day d-2 and earlier.

`_row_quantile` computes a different quantile level for every monitor in one sort, which is what makes the
adaptive loop fast. `interval_score` is the Winkler score: width plus a penalty for each miss. `uncertainty.run`
applies all of this to every model and reports coverage, width and score by slice and by month.

### 4.14 `alerts.py`: health warnings

The event is a 24-hour mean above 35.4 µg/m³, for the day after the forecast (hours 1 to 24) and the day after
that (25 to 48). `events` computes it, requiring at least 18 observed hours, and also marks the days that were
calm when the forecast was issued. `fit_classifiers` trains an XGBoost classifier for each event, with and without
neighbour features. `run` then scores every method: the classifiers by their probability, every forecasting model
by the mean of its forecast over the day, and persistence by the last 24-hour mean. Scores are PR-AUC, ROC-AUC and
the share of events caught when half of all alerts must be correct. `reliability` compares predicted probabilities
with observed frequencies.

### 4.15 `figures.py`, `plotting.py`, `report.py`, `export.py`

`plotting.py` defines one chart style and a fixed colour per model family, so a model has the same colour in every
figure. `figures.py` draws the eight result charts from the tables. `report.py` reads every table, computes the
numbers quoted in the text, and writes one self-contained HTML page with the figures embedded. `export.py` builds
the data bundle for the dashboard: all monitors, the result tables, and for 60 featured monitors the observations
and each model's day-ahead forecasts from late May to early July 2023.

### 4.16 `pipeline.py` and `run.py`

`pipeline.STAGES` maps each stage name to a title and a function. `run.py` reads names from the command line and
runs them in order; `all` runs every stage. Stages that need optional packages import them inside the function,
so the rest of the pipeline works without PyTorch or the foundation-model packages.

## 5. The tests

`tests/test_smokeshift.py` builds a small synthetic panel (14 monitors, 150 days, a daily cycle, one travelling
plume, 3% missing), so the tests need no download and run in seconds.

| Test | What it guarantees |
|---|---|
| `test_tabular_features_ignore_the_future` | Corrupting all data after a cut-off changes no tree feature before it |
| `test_spatial_features_ignore_the_future` | The same for neighbour features and channels |
| `test_naive_forecasts_ignore_the_future` | The same for the three reference forecasts |
| `test_transformer_inputs_ignore_the_future` | The same for the transformer's inputs, covariates and anchor |
| `test_targets_are_strictly_after_the_issue_time` | Targets start one hour after the issue time and end 48 hours after |
| `test_real_splits_do_not_overlap` | Train, validation and test targets are disjoint on the real panel |
| `test_fill_context_only_looks_back` | Gap filling uses earlier values only |
| `test_adaptive_conformal_recovers_coverage_after_a_shift` | Adaptive intervals return to 80% after the noise triples; static ones do not |
| `test_pinball_and_interval_score` | The scores match hand calculations |
| `test_benjamini_hochberg_known_values` | The FDR procedure matches a worked example |
| `test_panel_storage_round_trip` | Saving and loading the panel loses at most rounding to 0.1 |
| `test_distance_matrix` | Distances and bearings match known values |
| `test_api_reference_is_current` | `docs/API_REFERENCE.md` matches the code |

The first four are the ones that make the results trustworthy: they would fail if any model input could see the
future.

## 6. Every output file

`data/processed/`

| File | Contents |
|---|---|
| `panel.npz` | the monitor-by-hour matrix (int16 tenths of µg/m³) and its start time |
| `stations.csv` | one row per monitor: site code, location, state, county, region, per-year completeness, mean and hours over the threshold |
| `panel_summary.json` | row counts, monitors kept, share missing |
| `raw_manifest.json` | name, URL, size and SHA-256 of each raw file |

`outputs/tables/`

| File | Contents |
|---|---|
| `eda.json` | panel summary, weekday-effect counts, correlogram, principal-component summary, figure names |
| `eda_shift_by_region.csv` | level and tail statistics by region and year |
| `eda_paired_shift_test.csv` | Wilcoxon test of 2023 against each other year, by region |
| `eda_distribution_distance.csv` | KS statistic, Wasserstein distance and tail ratio against the training period |
| `eda_plume_lags.csv` | hours by which each city trails Minneapolis in the late-June 2023 plume |
| `gbm_tuning.json` | every random-search trial and the winner |
| `gbm_training.json` | rows, rounds, validation loss, settings and SHAP summary per tree model |
| `neural_training.json` | parameters, epochs, loss history and device per transformer |
| `scores_by_regime.csv` | MAE, bias, MASE and WQL per model for the five masks |
| `scores_by_slice.csv` | the same by horizon bucket, test year and region |
| `relative_mae_bootstrap.csv` | error relative to damped persistence with 95% intervals |
| `mae_by_horizon_*.csv` | MAE at each of 48 horizons, for four masks |
| `bias_by_outcome.csv` | mean error grouped by the air-quality category later observed |
| `evaluation_summary.json` | models, issue days, cells scored |
| `intervals.csv`, `intervals_monthly.csv` | coverage, width and interval score by model, method, slice and month |
| `alerts.csv`, `alerts_detail.json` | alert skill per method; classifier training details and reliability |
| `figures.json` | names of the result figures |

`outputs/figures/` holds thirteen PNG charts, numbered in the order they appear in the report.
`outputs/report.html` is the write-up.

## 7. The dashboard

`dashboard/page.html` is one page with no build step. It loads D3 and topojson from a CDN, then `states.js` and
`data.js`. It draws a map of all monitors, a time series for a chosen monitor with any model's forecasts, a
leaderboard that can be switched between the four slices, an error-by-horizon chart and an alert-skill chart.
Colours come from CSS variables, so the page follows the viewer's light or dark theme. `index.html` is the same
page wrapped for opening directly from disk.

## 8. How to extend the project

**Add a model.** Write a function that returns quantiles of shape `[538, 729, 48, 9]` (or a point forecast of
shape `[538, 729, 48]`) for `bench.issue_times("test")`, with `NaN` where `bench.eligible` is false. Call
`store.save(name, point, quantiles, info)`. Add a stage to `pipeline.STAGES` and a colour to
`plotting.MODEL_STYLE`. Run `evaluate uncertainty alerts figures report dashboard`.

**Add a feature for the trees.** Add it to the dictionary in `features.base` (or to `spatial.features`). It must
use only values at or before the issue time; the leakage tests will tell you if it does not.

**Change the experiment.** Edit `config.py`: the years, the split dates, the context, the horizon or the threshold.
Then rerun from `panel` (if the years changed) or from `naive`.

**Use another region or pollutant.** Change `EPA_URL` to another parameter file and `NOT_CONUS` in `panel.py`.

## 9. Glossary

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| PM2.5 | particles smaller than 2.5 micrometres, in µg/m³ |
| Issue time | the moment a forecast is made; here 12:00 UTC each day |
| Context | the history a model may look at; here 168 hours |
| Horizon | how far ahead a forecast is; here 1 to 48 hours |
| Quantile forecast | a value the truth should fall below with a stated probability |
| Pinball loss | the score that a correct quantile forecast minimises |
| WQL | weighted quantile loss: pinball loss summed over quantiles, divided by the sum of the truth |
| MAE | mean absolute error |
| MASE | MAE divided by the in-sample error of the seasonal naive forecast at the same monitor |
| Distribution shift | test data that differ systematically from training data |
| Global model | one model trained on all series, instead of one model per series |
| Zero-shot | using a pretrained model without training it on the task's data |
| Conformal prediction | a way to turn any forecast into an interval with guaranteed average coverage |
| Coverage | the share of true values that fall inside the interval |
| PR-AUC | area under the precision-recall curve; suited to rare events |
| Onset | an unhealthy period that begins when the previous 24 hours were clean |
| Forecaster's dilemma | scoring only extreme outcomes rewards forecasts that always predict extremes |
| SHAP | a method that attributes a prediction to each input feature |
| EOF | empirical orthogonal function: a principal component of a space-time field |
